where: Bookmark view (q1-bookmark, q2-pins), layer Key Places in the Union March to Vicksburg; Grant's route, step 1 and the Measure step
what: The sheet says Milliken's Bend is 'at the top edge of the view'. I open the bookmark and it is not there. I can see New Carthage and Hard Times. Bruinsburg Bend is a pin at the very bottom with no name showing, and Edwards is far right (under the legend if the legend is open). I only found all five in the picture of the map when it first opens, before I clicked the bookmark.
why: Step 1 of the first thing I do sends me to a view that hides two or three of the five pins. I'd think the map was broken and ask the teacher, and I can't measure Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend if I can't see either name.
suggestion: Reset the bookmark to the opening extent (all six pins visible, like the 'open' picture), or add a step: 'Zoom out one click until you can see all five dark pins.'
evidence: the-battle-of-vicksburg--q1-bookmark.png and --q2-pins.png (no Miliken's Bend pin, Bruinsburg Bend label cut off at bottom) versus --open.png (all pins visible). Sheet: 'spelled Miliken's Bend on the map, at the top edge of the view'.

where: Student sheet, Grant's route, Answer and step 3
what: The answer part is three questions in one: which side is each of five places on, how far south, and why didn't he cross at Vicksburg. There is one line to write on. Nothing on the map tells me why he did not cross at Vicksburg. And 'Use Measure' doesn't say how: where do I click, do I go in a straight line or follow the river?
why: I don't know how much to write, and the 'why' part I would have to guess. I'd probably answer the first bit and skip the rest.
suggestion: Split into three short answer lines: 'West side: ___ East side: ___', 'Distance: ___ miles', 'Why not cross at Vicksburg? (Hint: the Confederates had big guns on the hills above the river there.)' Add: 'Click Measure, click Milliken's Bend, then double-click Bruinsburg Bend (straight line).'
evidence: Sheet: 'Which side of the river is each place on? How far south of Milliken's Bend did Grant cross, and why did he not cross at Vicksburg itself?' followed by one measuring blank and one writing line.

where: Civil War Battlefields layer (q3-battles, q3-championhill, q4-partway); The battles of May 1863, steps 2-3 and Answer
what: When I turn the battles on there are diamonds all over, and none has a name until I click it. I have to click maybe seven or more, remember each name and date, then put them in date order on one line. Some diamonds near Vicksburg are probably not part of the May march (one north of Vicksburg is gray, one is over by Milliken's Bend), and I can't tell which ones count.
why: It's a lot of clicking and holding dates in my head, and I don't know when I'm done. This is where I'd run out of time or give up.
suggestion: Give a small table on the sheet with five rows (Battle / Date) and say 'There are five battles between 1 May and 17 May. Fill them in.' Or label the diamonds with their names on the map at this zoom. I'd also check whether Grand Gulf (the gray diamond by Hard Times) and the diamond north of Vicksburg have dates outside May 1863, since the heading says 'May 1863'.
evidence: the-battle-of-vicksburg--q3-battles.png (unlabelled diamonds), --q3-championhill.png (extra diamonds, including a gray one north of Vicksburg). Sheet: 'Which battles were fought between Bruinsburg Bend, Vicksburg and Jackson? List them in order by date.'

where: Battle pop-ups, Civil War Battlefields layer (q3-portgibson, q3-championhill, q4-porthudson)
what: The pop-up says 'Tap on image to view page' but there is no image, just a broken-picture icon with blue link text 'Battlefield Trust page'. There is also a long blank gap before the date.
why: It looks broken. If I click the link it takes me off the map to a website with a lot of reading, and I lose my place.
suggestion: Fix or remove the image in the pop-up; change the wording to a plain 'More about this battle (opens a new tab)' link, or leave the link out for students. Adding 'Result: Union victory' to the pop-up would also save the trip to the legend.
evidence: Pop-up text: 'Port Gibson ... May 1, 1863 / Battlefield Trust page / Tap on image to view page'; the-battle-of-vicksburg--q3-portgibson.png shows the broken image link.

where: Splitting the Confederacy, steps 1-2 (q4-partway, q4-porthudson); Civil War Battlefields layer
what: The sheet says 'click the diamond at Port Hudson', but the map has no name 'Port Hudson' on it. Zoomed out there are lots of blue diamonds in Louisiana. I'd have to click them one by one until a pop-up says Port Hudson. Zoomed out as far as Memphis to the Gulf they would be even smaller and closer together.
why: I can't find a place by name if the name isn't on the map. That's guessing, and I'd need help.
suggestion: Add Port Hudson as a named pin in the Key Places layer (or a 'Port Hudson' bookmark), or say on the sheet: 'It is the diamond on the river just north of Baton Rouge.'
evidence: the-battle-of-vicksburg--q4-partway.png (several unlabelled diamonds south and west of Natchez); --q4-porthudson.png (the basemap shows New Roads, Zachary, Baton Rouge but no Port Hudson label).

where: Splitting the Confederacy, Answer
what: 'When did Port Hudson end?' reads odd, because a place doesn't end. The pop-up just has two dates with a dash and doesn't say 'siege'. Then the last part, 'What could the Union control once Vicksburg and Port Hudson had both fallen?', needs me to know when Vicksburg fell, and nobody asked me to look that up.
why: I can copy 'July 9, 1863' but I'm not sure that's what is wanted, and the last question feels like a trick.
suggestion: Reword: 'On what date did the fighting at Port Hudson end? (It is the second date in the pop-up.)' and 'After both cities were captured, who controlled the whole Mississippi River?'
evidence: Pop-up text: 'Port Hudson ... May 21, 1863 – July 9, 1863'. Sheet: 'When did Port Hudson end? Which states lie west of the river? What could the Union control...'

where: Legend, Railroads 1826 to 1911 (open, q1-bookmark); Why Vicksburg?, step 3
what: I open the legend to find the railroad and it lists Transcontinental Railroad, Great Northern, Northern Pacific, Southern Pacific in pink and brown lines. None of those are on my map. The one I need is the last one, 'others', a very thin gray line, and on the map it is so faint next to the highway lines that I can hardly follow it east from Vicksburg.
why: The legend makes me look for pink lines that aren't there. The real line is easy to mix up with roads like I-20 and Highway 80.
suggestion: Give the railroad one darker, thicker symbol on this map and one legend entry called 'Railroad'; drop the western railroad names from this map's legend.
evidence: Legend text: 'Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific) / Great Northern / Northern Pacific / Southern Pacific / Transcontinental Railroad (Central Pacific) / others'; the-battle-of-vicksburg--q1-bookmark.png (faint dashed line beside I-20 and Highway 80).

where: Student sheet, Reading the map paragraph, and Why Vicksburg? Answer
what: 'Reading the map' is one block of six long sentences with a colon and semicolons. The first question, 'Why would both sides want Vicksburg?', has no hint about what to use from the map.
why: I skip long blocks, then I miss things like the battle layer being off. With no hint I'd write 'because it's important'.
suggestion: Turn Reading the map into four short bullets (yellow pin, dark pins, railroad, battle diamonds). Add a hint to the question: 'Use the river and the railroad in your answer.'
evidence: Sheet: 'Railroads are thin dark lines with short cross marks, like a track; they disappear if you zoom out too far, and they include lines built after the war.'

where: Bookmark and Jackson views (q1-jackson, q3-championhill), Key Places labels over basemap labels
what: The Edwards pin label sits right on top of the basemap's own 'Edwards', so it looks smudged, and in the opening view 'Miliken's Bend' runs into 'Tallulah' and 'Vicksburg'. The pin spelling 'Miliken's' is different from the sheet's 'Milliken's'.
why: Doubled words are hard to read for me, and two spellings make me wonder if it's the same place (the sheet does warn me, which helps).
suggestion: Fix the spelling in the layer to 'Milliken's Bend' and give the pin labels a white halo or an offset so they don't sit on the basemap names.
evidence: the-battle-of-vicksburg--q1-jackson.png (Edwards doubled), --open.png (Miliken's Bend label over Tallulah).

where: Pop-ups, Population in 1790 and House seats in 1793 layers (q1-virginia, q1-maryland); Who lived where in 1790?, step 3
what: The first line I'm told to read says Virginia is '39.099998474121094%' enslaved and Maryland '32.20000076293945%'. Delaware says '1 House seats' and '1 seats'.
why: I don't know how to read a number that long. Is it 39 or 39 million? This is the exact number the question is about.
suggestion: Round the percentage in the pop-up to a whole number ('39%') and fix the plural ('1 seat').
evidence: Pop-up text: '1790 census: 747,610 people, 292,627 of them enslaved (39.099998474121094%).'; 'That gave Delaware 1 House seats in 1793'; 'counted in full: 1 seats'.

where: Who lived where in 1790?, steps 2-3 and Answer
what: 'Click the pies and read each pop-up' means about fifteen pies, and each pop-up is four paragraphs. Then the question asks about 'more than a quarter', but the pop-up gives percents.
why: I might not know a quarter is 25%. Reading fifteen long pop-ups is where I'd stop. The small pies around Maryland, Delaware and New Jersey are also on top of each other, so they're hard to click.
suggestion: Say 'more than a quarter (25%)'. Tell me I only need the first line, and that the biggest pie is the state with the most people. Add 'Zoom in on the small pies in the middle' or point to a bookmark.
evidence: Sheet: 'In which states were more than a quarter of the people enslaved?'; we-the-people-1787-1791--q1-bookmark.png (overlapping pies at Maryland/Delaware/New Jersey).

where: House seats in 1793 layer, bookmark view (q2-seats); Seats in Congress, step 2 and Answer ('which the fewest?')
what: The sheet says to read the labels for the state and its seats. I can see VA: 19, PA: 13, NY: 10 and so on, but Delaware, Rhode Island and New Hampshire have no label at this zoom, and the Massachusetts label is cut off ('MA: 14' runs under the legend and sits on Maine). The lowest numbers I can read are 2 (GA, KY, VT), so I'd write one of those for 'fewest'.
why: The real smallest state doesn't show its number unless I zoom in or click it, and nothing tells me to. I'd get the answer wrong without knowing.
suggestion: Make every state's label show at the bookmark zoom (allow overlap or use leader lines for DE, RI, NH), or add a step: 'Zoom in on the small states: some labels only appear close up.'
evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q2-seats.png: labels MA: 14 (clipped), VT: 2, NY: 10, CT: 7, PA: 13, NJ: 5, MD: 8, VA: 19, KY: 2, NC: 10, SC: 6, GA: 2; none for DE, RI, NH. Delaware pop-up: '1 House seats'.

where: The three-fifths clause, Answer
what: The answer part is a long explaining sentence and then two questions with several bits each. There are fill-in blanks for Virginia but none for South Carolina. The last part, 'Which states gained seats by counting enslaved people', means clicking every state again and comparing three numbers each.
why: The Virginia blanks are great, I know exactly what to write. For South Carolina and 'which states gained' I don't know how much to write or when I'm finished.
suggestion: Add the same blank line for South Carolina. Change the last part to something with an end: 'Click Pennsylvania and Massachusetts too. Did their three numbers change? Name two states that gained seats.'
evidence: Sheet: 'Virginia: ___ seats with the three-fifths clause; ___ if counted in full; ___ if not counted at all.' with no matching line for South Carolina.

where: Ratifying the Constitution layer (q4-ratify, q4-delaware, q4-nc); How close was ratification?, steps 3-4
what: With the other two layers off, the state shapes are gone, so the pies float on a blank map with no state lines. The labels (VA 10, NC (1788), NC 12, SC 8) sit up and to the right of their pies, so each one looks like it belongs to the next pie along. 'SC 8' is right beside a North Carolina pie, and 'NC (1788)' is right beside what I think is Virginia's. In the north-east five or six pies are piled on top of each other.
why: I'm told to 'find North Carolina and click both of its pies', but I can't tell which two are North Carolina. I'd click the wrong ones. In the pile-up up north I can't click the ones underneath.
suggestion: Keep a plain state outline layer on under the ratification pies. Centre each label on or directly under its own pie. Tell students on the sheet to open the 'New England and New York' and 'The South' bookmarks for this question (they exist but the sheet never mentions them).
evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q4-ratify.png (no state outlines; labels offset; overlapping pies near NY 11 / RI 13); --q4-delaware.png (label 'NC 12' beside the orange-majority pie, 'SC 8' beside the blue North Carolina pie). Bookmarks listed: 'New England and New York', 'The South'.

where: Ratifying the Constitution pop-ups, first line (q4-delaware, q4-rhodeisland, q4-nc)
what: The first line says 'Ratified on 12/6/1787, 6:09 PM: 30 for, 0 against.' Every state says 6:09 PM. The votes I need come after a date and a clock time.
why: Three sets of numbers in one line. I could easily copy '6:09' or '12/6' as the vote. And a vote in 1787 at exactly 6:09 PM in every state looks wrong, so I'd stop trusting it.
suggestion: Show the date without a time and spelled out, with the vote first: '30 for, 0 against. Ratified December 7, 1787.' I'd check the Delaware date too: the first line says 12/6 but the convention line says it met 3-7 December, so the date may have slipped a day because of the time zone.
evidence: Pop-up text: 'Ratified on 12/6/1787, 6:09 PM: 30 for, 0 against.'; 'Ratified on 5/28/1790, 6:09 PM: 34 for, 32 against.'; 'Ratified on 11/20/1789, 6:09 PM: 194 for, 77 against.'

where: How close was ratification?, Answer ('Which three votes were closest?')
what: To find the three closest I have to click all fourteen or so pies, write down two numbers for each, and do a subtraction for each. The sheet gives me one line and no place to keep the numbers.
why: That's a lot of steps hidden inside one short question. I'd lose track and guess from the pies that look half and half.
suggestion: Say it is fine to start from the pies that look nearly half blue, half orange: 'Find the pies that are close to half and half. Click those and write the votes: ___ for, ___ against.' Give three short lines.
evidence: Sheet: 'Click the pies and read the first line of each pop-up: the votes for and against.' / 'Which three votes were closest?'; we-the-people-1787-1791--q4-ratify.png.

where: Student sheet, Before you start and Reading the map
what: Words that stop me: 'ratified', 'delegates', 'convention', 'compromise', 'clause'. 'Ratify' is in the title, the layer name and the last question and it is never explained. Reading the map is one paragraph of seven sentences about three different layers.
why: If I don't know 'ratify' I can't do question 4 or the big question at all.
suggestion: Add a three-word box: 'ratify = vote to accept', 'delegate = person sent to speak for a state', 'convention = big meeting'. Break Reading the map into one bullet per layer.
evidence: Sheet: 'The Constitution would take effect only when nine states had ratified it, each at a special convention.'

where: Legend and Map layers list (open, q2-seats, q4-ratify)
what: The legend has headings like 'Total1790', 'HouseSeats' and 'Total', and a gray 'Other' dot that isn't on the map. The layer list also has 'House seats today (2020 apportionment)', which the sheet never uses, and the layer names are longer than the ones on the sheet.
why: Run-together words and extra things make me think I'm in the wrong place. For the ratifying pies, nothing tells me what a bigger pie means (I'd guess more people, but I think it is more votes).
suggestion: Rename the legend headings 'People in 1790', 'Seats in the House', 'Votes cast at the convention'; remove 'Other'; either use the today layer in a step or say 'you don't need House seats today'.
evidence: Legend text: 'Total1790', 'HouseSeats', 'Total', 'Other'. Layers list: 'House seats today (2020 apportionment) (off)'.

where: Opening view (open); Who represents us?, step 1
what: The map opens on all of North America covered in thick blue lines, so many that the middle of the country is nearly solid blue and the city names are hidden. The sheet just says 'Zoom to your town'. It doesn't mention a search box, so I have to guess where my town is and zoom and drag.
why: I'm quick with a map on my phone because I type the place. Here I may not know where my town is on a US map, and that's the very first step.
suggestion: If the app has a search tool, say 'Type your town in Search'. If not, add 'Find your state first, then zoom in' and have the teacher share a link or bookmark for the school's town. Thinner district lines at the national zoom would help too.
evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--open.png (dense blue lines over the eastern US); sheet: 'Zoom to your town; the basemap has place names.' Tools listed do not include a search.

where: State view (q1-state), Congressional districts layer; Who represents us?, step 4 and Answer ('How many districts does your state have?')
what: When I zoom out to the whole state, the district lines and the state border are the same blue line. No district has a number on it. Around the cities the districts are tiny and squiggly. I can't tell where Ohio stops and Indiana or Pennsylvania starts, so I can't count.
why: The only way to count would be clicking every shape and reading its number, and I'd still not know if I missed one. I'd guess or copy someone.
suggestion: Label each district with its number at state zoom, and draw state borders in a different, heavier line. Or change the question: 'Click a few districts near yours. What is the highest district number you can find in your state?'
evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q1-state.png (unnumbered districts, state and district boundaries drawn in the same blue). Legend text: 'Congressional district' only.

where: Town view (q2-buildings), basemap; Rights in public places, steps 1-2
what: The sheet says zoom in 'until the basemap shows building names' and find a courthouse, city hall, library, place of worship, polling place or newspaper office. In the downtown picture the names I can read are an arena, a stadium, colleges, a hospital, parks and a train station. No courthouse, no city hall, no library. I don't think a map ever labels a polling place or a newspaper office.
why: I'd keep zooming and dragging looking for words that may never show up. If I don't already know where the courthouse is in my town, I'm stuck on step 2.
suggestion: Tell me how far to zoom ('until you can see single buildings') and give the fallback: 'If the name isn't on the map, ask where it is or use the street address.' Take polling place and newspaper office off the 'find it on the map' list, or say 'your school may be a polling place'. A point layer of public buildings would be the real fix.
evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q2-buildings.png (labels: Nationwide Arena, Lower.com Stadium, Columbus State Community College, Franklin University, Capitol Square, Columbus Commons; no courthouse, city hall or library label). Whether a closer zoom shows them is not in the pictures.

where: Rights in public places, steps 3-4; Responsibilities, steps 2-3
what: 'Use Sketch to put a pin on each one' and 'Next to each pin, write a right' don't tell me which button in Sketch makes a pin or how to add words. I also don't know what happens when I click the map to drop a pin: I think the district pop-up will open on top.
why: I'm fine with apps but I'd be poking at buttons, and there are at least seven pins and seven labels to make across two questions. Sketches aren't saved, so if I close the tab I lose it all.
suggestion: Add two mini-steps: 'In Sketch choose the point (pin) tool and click the building. Then choose the text tool and click next to the pin to type.' Or let me write the right on the paper sheet in a four-row table (Place / Right) instead of typing on the map.
evidence: Sheet: 'Use Sketch to put a pin on each one.' 'Next to each pin, write a right from the Bill of Rights that people use there.' 'Finish in one lesson or take a screenshot, because sketches are not saved.'

where: Responsibilities, steps 1-3 and Answer
what: I'm asked to pin where people vote, do jury service and pay taxes. I don't know what jury service is or where you pay taxes, and the map doesn't show polling places or tax offices.
why: I can't pin a place I can't find and don't know. I'd write 'courthouse' for all three.
suggestion: Give a hint line for each: 'Jury service (helping decide a court case): courthouse. Voting: often a school, library or church. Taxes: city hall or the post office.' Say two pins are enough.
evidence: Sheet: 'Add a pin at each place where people carry out a citizen's responsibility: voting, jury service, paying taxes.'

where: National Register of Historic Places layer (q4-nrhp, q4-nrhp-click); History where we live, steps 2-3
what: With the layer on, downtown is covered in tiny dark diamonds, all nearly the same dark green. There are dozens, and along one street they run together in a row. I'm told to click 'the two nearest your school', but first I have to find my school on the map, and the diamonds are small to hit. The legend colours for district and site (two dark reds) look alike, and object and structure are both pale.
why: Finding my school and then judging 'nearest' among dozens of same-looking dots takes me a long time. If my school is out of town there may be none near it.
suggestion: Make the diamonds bigger when zoomed in. Change the step to 'Click two diamonds near your school or in your town centre.' Tell me to read 'Resource Type' in the pop-up and not rely on colour.
evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp.png (dozens of same-colour diamonds in downtown Columbus). Legend text: 'building / structure / district / site / object'.

where: Historic place pop-up (q4-nrhp-click)
what: The pop-up has the name and address at the top, which is good, then 'Property ID: 72001011', 'Status: Listed', 'National Register Information Tracking System Reference Number: 72001011' and 'National Archive Information'. It says '1 of 2' at the bottom because the district shape is under it.
why: Half the pop-up is numbers and long official words I don't need. I'd wonder if I'm supposed to write them down.
suggestion: Cut the pop-up to name, address and 'Type: building', with the reference number and archive link in small print at the bottom.
evidence: Pop-up text: 'Ohio Statehouse / Property ID: 72001011 / ... / Resource Type: building / Status: Listed / National Register Information Tracking System Reference Number: 72001011 / National Archive Information'.

where: Whole student sheet: four questions, Your answer, Looking back
what: This sheet has me find my town, count districts, find and pin at least seven places and type a label by each, then find my school and two historic places, then choose three places and explain. Every answer has one writing line.
why: I couldn't finish this in one class, and the sheet says my sketches vanish if I don't. Knowing that, I'd rush or stop.
suggestion: Mark a short route: questions 1 and 2 are the core, and Responsibilities and History are 'if you have time'. Cut to three pins. Give tables to fill in (Place / Right) so I know how much to write.
evidence: Sheet: 'Find four public places', 'Add a pin at each place where people carry out a citizen's responsibility', 'click the two nearest your school', 'Choose the three places that best show rights and responsibilities... and explain your choices.'

where: Election of 1796 pop-up for Maryland (q1-maryland); The election of 1796, step 4 and Answer ('Which states split their votes, and how?')
what: The title says 'Maryland: 10 electors'. Then it says Adams 7, Jefferson 4. That's 11. Then it says the votes add up to twice the electors.
why: I'm asked how the state split. 7 and 4 don't make 10, so I'd think I read it wrong, or write '7 and 3'. The 'two votes each' idea is the hardest thing in this lesson and this is where it bites.
suggestion: Add one plain sentence to pop-ups where the two numbers don't add up to the electors: 'One elector voted for both Adams and Jefferson.' (I'd check that against the source.) On the sheet, warn: 'In Maryland the two numbers add up to 11, not 10. That is not a mistake.'
evidence: Pop-up text: 'Maryland: 10 electors / Electors' votes in 1796: John Adams 7, Thomas Jefferson 4, Thomas Pinckney 4, Aaron Burr 3, others 2. / ... In the pie: John Adams (Federalist), 7 votes; Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republican), 4 votes.'

where: Election pop-ups, both layers (q1-pie, q2-pennsylvania, q4-newyork)
what: Each pop-up gives the votes twice: first a list of four men (Adams, Jefferson, Pinckney, Burr), then 'In the pie: John Adams (Federalist), 1 votes; Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republican), 14 votes.' In between is a sentence about votes adding up to twice the electors. The 1800 ones add a paragraph about the tie with Burr, the House and the 12th Amendment.
why: I only need two numbers and they are in the middle of the second paragraph. The first list has four names and I don't know who Pinckney and Burr are, so I'm not sure which numbers to use. '1 votes' looks like a mistake.
suggestion: Put the two pie numbers first, in bold, on their own line: 'Adams 1, Jefferson 14.' Move the other candidates and the 12th Amendment note below, smaller. Fix '1 votes' to '1 vote'.
evidence: Pop-up text: 'Electors' votes in 1796: John Adams 1, Thomas Jefferson 14, Thomas Pinckney 2, Aaron Burr 13. / Each elector cast two votes for president, so the votes add up to twice the number of electors. In the pie: John Adams (Federalist), 1 votes; ...'

where: Bookmark view, both election layers (q1-courts-off, q2-1800); Q1 step 4, Q2 steps 2-3, Q4 step 3
what: Around Maryland, Delaware and New Jersey three pies sit on top of each other. I can see Maryland's two-colour pie and two orange ones squashed against it, but I can't tell which is Delaware and which is New Jersey, or whether one is hiding a slice.
why: I'm told to 'click each two-color pie'. If one is hidden under another I'll miss it, and clicking in a pile gets me the wrong state. There are no names on the map to check against.
suggestion: Add a bookmark zoomed on the middle states (Pennsylvania to Maryland) and name it in the step, or nudge the Delaware and New Jersey pies apart, or add two-letter state labels to the pies.
evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--q1-courts-off.png and --q2-1800.png (overlapping pies east of the Maryland pie).

where: Election of 1800 layer (q2-1800); The election of 1800, Answer ('Which state was the closest?')
what: In 1800 Maryland's pie looks exactly half orange, half blue, and Pennsylvania's pop-up says 8 to 7. So is 'the closest' Maryland (a tie) or Pennsylvania (one apart)? The question wants one state.
why: I don't know which the teacher wants, and a tie might not count as 'close' in my head. I'd stall on it.
suggestion: Ask it in two parts: 'Which state was split exactly in half? Which state was split by just one vote?'
evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--q2-1800.png (Maryland pie half and half); pop-up text: 'In the pie: John Adams (Federalist), 7 votes; Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republican), 8 votes.' (Pennsylvania 1800).

where: Did one state decide the election?, steps 1-3 and Answer
what: The question says 'If New York had voted as it did in 1796, what would the totals have been?' The steps only tell me to click New York in 1800. Nobody tells me to go back and check how New York voted in 1796, or that I should take 12 off Jefferson and add 12 to Adams. Then 'Which other states were close enough to change the result?' I don't know what 'close enough' means in numbers.
why: It's a maths problem inside a long sentence with a 'what if'. The blanks help, but I don't know how to get the numbers that go in them. I'd leave the second question empty.
suggestion: Add steps: 'Turn on 1796 and click New York: who got its 12 votes then? Now take 12 away from Jefferson's 73 and add 12 to Adams's 65.' Swap the last part for 'Jefferson won by 8. Name one other state with 8 or more electors where the vote was split.' or drop it.
evidence: Sheet: 'In 1800 Jefferson won 73 electors' votes and Adams 65. If New York had voted as it did in 1796, what would the totals have been? Which other states were close enough to change the result?'; pop-up text: 'New York: 12 electors ... Thomas Jefferson 12, Aaron Burr 12.'

where: Which states switched?, step 3 and Answer
what: The answer part has three questions, and the third ('Using both maps, where was each party strong and where did the two parties compete?') is the same as the big question. where: Massachusetts bookmark, Revolutionary War Battles and Turning Points layers; sheet question 1 step 4 and From the front step 5
what: The sheet says 'Click the Boston diamond and read its dates'. At the bookmark I can't see a Boston diamond: numbered circle 2 sits on top of it. When I click there I get a pop-up headed 'Battle Details', titled 'Battle of Bunker Hill', dated just '1775', ending 'Victor: Britain', and the counter says '1 of 4'. The siege of Boston with its two dates is somewhere behind three more arrow clicks. The sheet only warns about circles covering diamonds in question 4.
why: Question 1 is my warm-up, done live in front of the class. If my first click on Boston shows a different battle, the wrong year format and a British win, half the room writes that down, and I burn minutes of a 45-minute period paging through four pop-ups. Students on phones will not find it at all.
suggestion: Move circle 2 off the Boston diamond, or make the Turning Points layer not clickable until question 4, or have the Massachusetts bookmark open below the zoom where circles show. Failing that, add to question 1 step 4: 'Circle 2 covers the Boston diamond: click it and use the arrow until the title says Siege of Boston.'
evidence: revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q1-bookmark.png (circles 1 and 2, only one blue diamond visible near them); revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q1-boston.png, pop-up text 'Battle Details / Battle of Bunker Hill / 1775 ... Victor: Britain', counter '1 of 4'

where: View one zoom step out from the Massachusetts bookmark, Thirteen British Colonies labels; sheet question 2 step 3 and the answer notes for question 2

I can't see a Rhode Island or New Jersey label at this zoom (New Jersey's is under the diamonds when the map opens), and the two blue diamonds on Lake Champlain sit right beside the New Hampshire label although the key says New York.

suggestion: Put the colony in each battle pop-up ('Massachusetts', 'New York', 'Province of Quebec') so the date and the colony come from the same click, or add a label point for Massachusetts near Boston and make sure Rhode Island and New Jersey labels draw at this zoom. where: Question 2 (the 'If you only do one' question), sheet steps 1-2 and From the front steps 2-5
what: Students are meant to click all 21 diamonds and sort them by year. At the zoom the sheet gives, the New York diamonds are a pile of four or five touching each other and the Boston ones are three on top of each other; my click on Bunker Hill came up '1 of 3'. The From the front version clicks only Bunker Hill and Brooklyn and then asks 'which colonies had battles in 1775, and which in 1776?', which two clicks cannot answer. Color shows the winner, not the year.
why: This is the one question I would pick for a single period, and it is the one that does not work from one screen with the class on paper. Twenty-one pop-ups from the front is all 15 minutes and more, and kids on phones cannot pick one diamond out of the pile.
suggestion: Give me a printable class table (battle name, blank date, blank colony, blank winner) so pairs fill it in while I click, and rewrite From the front to click one battle per region per year (say six clicks) that are enough to show the pattern. On the map, a second symbol or label for the year (1775 hollow, 1776 solid) would let the whole class see the shift without any clicking.
evidence: revolutionary-battles-1775-1776--q2-all.png (overlapping diamonds at New York and Boston); --q2-bunkerhill.png (counter '1 of 3'); From the front steps 'Click the Bunker Hill diamond... Click the Brooklyn diamond... Ask: which colonies had battles in 1775, and which in 1776?'

where: Zoomed in on New York City with circles showing; sheet question 4 step 3 and From the front steps 3-4

where: Reading the map paragraph on the sheet; Turning Points pop-ups (questions 1 and 4)
what: The sheet says a battle's pop-up gives 'not the winner in words: the diamond's color shows the winner'. where: Indigenous Territories layer zoomed in on Wyoming and Nebraska; sheet question 3 steps 2-4; answer notes question 3
what: The names that appear are small pale letters on the shading, and several are in the nations' own languages: 'Tséstho’e (Cheyenne)', 'Oohenumpa', 'Sicangu', 'Mnicoujou', 'Pa’ka’to de uk’ethi (Ponca)'. In both pictures the shading also stops at dead-straight edges, which the capture note puts down to the map not having finished drawing.
why: From the front I am supposed to be 'reading out the names it crosses'. I cannot pronounce some of them, the back row cannot read them, and when a pair writes 'Sicangu' I cannot check it against my notes. If the layer draws as slowly for my students as it did for the capture, they will see squares, not territories.
suggestion: Add to the answer notes the names that actually show along the Oregon Trail at the zoom students use, with a pronunciation hint and the common English name (for example Sicangu: a Lakota band, also called Brulé; worth checking). where: Railroads 1826 to 1911 layer at the bookmark and at the opening view; sheet question 1 step 3; From the front question 1 step 3

suggestion: Add to sheet question 4 and From the front: 'Open the New England and New York bookmark to separate the northern pies, then The South'. Add a hint that the closest votes are the pies nearest half blue, half orange-red, so students click those first.

where: Congressional districts layer zoomed out to a whole state (q1-state); sheet question 1 step 4; From the front question 1 steps 5 and 6
what: The sheet asks how many districts my state has, and the notes say to count the blue-outlined areas with the whole state on screen. In the Ohio picture the state border is the same blue line as the district lines, the neighboring states' districts are drawn the same way, and the city districts around Columbus, Cleveland and Cincinnati are tiny shapes. I cannot count 15 from that picture with confidence, and the notes give examples of 52, 38 and 28 for the big states.
why: It is the 'if you only do one' question. In a large state with a big city, which is where a school like mine is, the count cannot be done from a projector and would eat the period on Chromebooks. The first half of the question works; the second half stalls.
suggestion: Add state outlines in a different color and weight so the state stands out from its districts, and put the district number as a label inside each district so the highest number can be read instead of counted. Or change the question to 'click three more districts in your state: are they the same party as yours?' and give the state's seat count in the notes.

where: Topographic basemap zoomed in on a town (q2-buildings); sheet question 2 steps 1 and 2; From the front question 2 step 2
what: The sheet says to zoom in until the basemap shows building names and find a courthouse, city hall, library, place of worship, polling place or newspaper office. In the downtown Columbus picture the names I can read are an arena, a stadium, colleges, a hospital, schools, parks and the train station. I do not see a courthouse, a city hall, a library or a church named, and no basemap is going to label a polling place or a newspaper office.
why: Students will scroll around looking for labels that are not there. My students know their own blocks, so they can still pin from memory, but the sheet sets them up to search the map first, and in 12 minutes on a shared device that search is most of the time.
suggestion: Reword the sheet: 'Think of four public places you know. Find each on the map using street names and landmarks; some will not be labeled.' In the teacher notes, say plainly that polling places and newspaper offices are never labeled, and suggest the teacher bring a short list of local addresses.
