what: The diamonds have no names on the map, so the only way to know a battle is to click it. In the bookmark view with the layer on, Port Gibson's diamond is half hidden at the bottom edge, there is a blue diamond north-west of Vicksburg near Richmond and a grey one north of the city, and the diamonds toward Jackson are off the east edge. The sheet says 'click the diamonds between Bruinsburg Bend and Vicksburg' without saying how many or that some nearby diamonds are from other months.
why: My students will click every diamond they see and copy every name and date. The extra ones (I would check what the diamonds north and north-west of Vicksburg are, and their dates) will end up in their lists, and each click is more English to read. They also do not know when they have found them all.
suggestion: Say in step 2 how many battles to find ('find six battles dated May 1863; ignore diamonds with other months') and tell students to drag the map east. Better still, label the campaign's diamonds with their names on the map.
evidence: the-battle-of-vicksburg--q3-battles.png (unlabeled diamonds at top left, at Grand Gulf and at the bottom edge); --q3-championhill.png (grey diamond north of Vicksburg); sheet: 'Click the diamonds between Bruinsburg Bend and Vicksburg and read their dates.'

where: Spanish student sheet, question 4 (step 3 and the answer line)
what: The Spanish says 'Lee cuándo terminó el sitio de Port Hudson' and then '¿Cuándo terminó Port Hudson?'. In everyday Spanish 'sitio' means place, so my students read 'when the place of Port Hudson ended', and the second version (also odd in English: 'When did Port Hudson end?') has no noun at all. The pop-up itself never uses the word siege; it only gives two dates.
why: Siege is the key idea of this question and the word that explains why there are two dates. With 'sitio' and no gloss, students do not get it, and they do not know which of the two dates to write.
suggestion: Use 'asedio' and gloss it once: 'el asedio (siege: rodear una ciudad hasta que se rinde)'. Change the question to '¿Cuándo terminó el asedio de Port Hudson?' and the English to 'When did the siege of Port Hudson end?'. Add 'the second date in the pop-up is the day it ended'.
evidence: Spanish sheet: 'Lee cuándo terminó el sitio de Port Hudson.' and '¿Cuándo terminó Port Hudson?'; pop-up text: 'Port Hudson ... May 21, 1863 – July 9, 1863'

where: Spanish student sheet, question 1 answer line and question 2
what: Question 1 asks '¿Por qué querrían Vicksburg ambos lados?' and the very next question asks '¿De qué lado del río está cada lugar?'. The same word, lado, means the two armies in one question and the river banks in the next.
why: A student can easily answer question 1 about the two sides of the river. For the two armies Spanish uses 'bandos', and for a river 'orilla' is clearer.
suggestion: Question 1: '¿Por qué querrían Vicksburg ambos bandos (la Unión y la Confederación)?'. Question 2: '¿En qué orilla del río (este u oeste) está cada alfiler?'. The big question would also read more naturally as '¿Por qué necesitaba la Unión tomar Vicksburg y cómo lo logró Grant?'.
evidence: Spanish sheet: '¿Por qué querrían Vicksburg ambos lados?'; '¿De qué lado del río está cada lugar?'

where: Question 4 steps 1, 2 and 4, zoomed out (q4-partway, q4-porthudson)
what: Zoomed out part-way, there are many identical unlabeled diamonds south of Vicksburg and no label that says Port Hudson, so finding 'the diamond at Port Hudson' is trial and error. No state names show in that picture either. The full view from Memphis to the Gulf was not captured, so I am inferring that it is at least as crowded. The Spanish sheet writes Misisipi, Luisiana and golfo de México, but the map writes Mississippi River and (I assume) Louisiana.
why: English learners match words on the sheet to words on the screen. There is nothing on screen to match for Port Hudson, and the state names they must copy are spelled differently from the ones on their sheet.
suggestion: Add a second bookmark for this question ('The Mississippi from Memphis to the Gulf') and a named pin or label for Port Hudson. In the Spanish sheet give the map's spelling once: 'Luisiana (Louisiana)', 'río Misisipi (Mississippi River)'. Tell students which landmark to use: 'the diamond just north of Baton Rouge'.
evidence: the-battle-of-vicksburg--q4-partway.png (unlabeled diamonds, no state names); --q4-porthudson.png (basemap shows Baton Rouge and New Roads, no Port Hudson label); capture note that the full view could not be captured

where: Civil War Battlefields pop-ups (q3-portgibson, q3-championhill, q4-porthudson)
what: Under the date each pop-up shows a broken picture with the link text 'Battlefield Trust page' and 'Tap on image to view page'. The pop-up does not say who won; that is only in the diamond's color, and once a diamond is clicked it turns bright blue so its color is gone. The legend's yellow 'Inconclusive' diamond is the same yellow as the Vicksburg pin.
why: The broken picture may only be the capture, but if students see it they will ask what is wrong. Clicking through leads to a long English web page. The sheet tells them the result is in the legend, but they have to close the pop-up to see the color again.
suggestion: Add a 'Result' line to the pop-up (Union victory / Confederate victory) and check the picture loads in the app. If the link stays, the sheet could say 'you do not need the picture link'.
evidence: pop-up text: 'Port Gibson ... May 1, 1863 / Battlefield Trust page / Tap on image to view page'; the-battle-of-vicksburg--q3-portgibson.png shows the broken image and the highlighted diamond

where: Teacher notes, Key words; student sheets, Reading the map
what: The key words (siege, campaign, bluff, gunboat, supply line, surrender) are a bare list in the teacher notes: no definitions, no Spanish, and bluff, gunboat and supply line never appear on the student sheet. Reading the map is one block of about 95 words (longer in Spanish) that mixes symbols, a warning about railroads built after the war, and an instruction to turn a layer on.
why: I need key words on the page my students hold, with a short meaning in both languages. A solid paragraph before the first question is where my newer English learners lose the thread.
suggestion: Put a small word box on both sheets with the words students actually meet (siege / asedio, surrender / rendirse, railroad / ferrocarril, victory / victoria) and a one-line meaning. Set Reading the map as a short list, one symbol per line.
evidence: Teacher notes: 'Key words: siege, campaign, bluff, gunboat, supply line, surrender'; student sheet Reading the map paragraph

where: Lesson page, Student activity section (note under the sheet)
what: The lesson page says 'Español: Spanish draft for review by a native speaker.' The Word sheet my students get does not carry that note.
why: I use the Spanish sheet in class, so I need to know whether it has been reviewed. Most of it is good, but the points above (sitio, lados, '¿Cuándo terminó Port Hudson?') are the kind a native reviewer would catch.
suggestion: Have the Spanish reviewed before release and remove the draft note, or say on the page which version has been reviewed.
evidence: Lesson page: 'Español: Spanish draft for review by a native speaker. Layer and bookmark names stay in English, as they appear in MapMaker.'

where: Ratifying the Constitution layer at the bookmark view (q4-ratify); question 4 steps 3 and 4
what: With the other layers off, the state outlines disappear and the pies float on a blank coast. The labels sit up and to the right of their pies, so at this zoom they land beside the wrong pie: 'NC (1788)' sits on a half-and-half pie further north, 'NC 12' sits beside the mostly orange pie, and 'SC 8' sits beside a mostly blue pie that is not South Carolina's. In the north-east the pies for New York, Rhode Island, Vermont, New Hampshire, Massachusetts and Connecticut are stacked on top of each other and several labels are missing. The map has two bookmarks made for this (New England and New York; The South) but the sheet never mentions them.
why: My students cannot read a state from its shape, so the labels are all they have, and here the labels point to the wrong pies. 'Find North Carolina and click both of its pies' becomes guesswork, and the three closest votes are in the stacked north-east cluster.
suggestion: Add to question 4: 'Open the New England and New York bookmark, then The South bookmark.' Put each label directly on or under its pie, keep the state outlines visible with this layer, and tell students the pop-up title names the state.
evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q4-ratify.png (label positions and overlapping pies); --q4-nc.png (zoomed in, labels sit up-right of each pie); bookmarks list: 'The states in 1790, New England and New York, The South'

where: House seats in 1793 layer, labels at the bookmark view (q2-seats); question 2 answer 'which the fewest'
what: The labels show VT: 2, KY: 2, GA: 2, NJ: 5, MD: 8 and so on, but there is no visible label for Delaware (DE: 1), Rhode Island or New Hampshire, and MA: 14 sits up in Maine. The step says 'Read the labels' to find the fewest seats.
why: Reading only the labels, a student will write Vermont, Kentucky or Georgia with 2 as the fewest. The answer notes want Delaware with 1. Delaware is a sliver on this map and hard to click.
suggestion: Make the DE, RI and NH labels always draw (offset with a leader line if needed), or add a hint to step 2: 'zoom in on the small states between Maryland and New Jersey'.
evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q2-seats.png (no DE, RI or NH label); answer notes: 'Delaware, DE: 1, the fewest'

where: Spanish student sheet, questions 3 and 4 (state names)
what: The Spanish steps say 'Haz clic en Virginia y en Carolina del Sur' and 'Busca Carolina del Norte', but the map has no place names; what students see is SC: 6, NC: 10, 'NC (1788)', 'NC 12', and pop-up titles 'South Carolina in 1790' and 'North Carolina: 12th state to ratify'. The sheet never gives the English name or the abbreviation.
why: The whole point of the bilingual sheet is that a student can match the Spanish step to what is on screen. Carolina del Sur does not look like SC or South Carolina to a newcomer.
suggestion: Give both the first time each state is named: 'Virginia (VA) y Carolina del Sur (South Carolina, SC)', 'Carolina del Norte (North Carolina, NC)'. Do the same for Nueva York if it is used.
evidence: Spanish sheet: 'Haz clic en Virginia y en Carolina del Sur.' and 'Busca Carolina del Norte y haz clic en sus dos gráficos.'; map labels in we-the-people-1787-1791--q2-seats.png and --q4-ratify.png

where: Population pop-up, first line (q1-virginia, q1-maryland); question 1 step 3
what: The first line, which the sheet tells students to read for the percentage, shows 'enslaved (39.099998474121094%)' for Virginia and '(32.20000076293945%)' for Maryland. South Carolina and Delaware show clean numbers (43%, 15%). The teacher notes say to accept the rounded figure, but the student sheet says nothing.
why: My students copy what they see. A 17-digit number looks like a different kind of number altogether, and some will not see it is 39 percent, which is the whole comparison with 'more than a quarter'.
suggestion: Fix the pop-up to show one decimal place (39.1%). Until then add to step 3 in both languages: 'If the percentage has many digits, use only the first two (39%).'
evidence: pop-up text: '1790 census: 747,610 people, 292,627 of them enslaved (39.099998474121094%).'; we-the-people-1787-1791--q1-virginia.png

where: Both student sheets, question 3 (answer prompt and fill-in line)
what: The answer prompt is four sentences with three questions and two 'if ... had been' conditions, followed by a single fill-in line for Virginia only. South Carolina and the 'other states' have nowhere to go but one blank writing line.
why: This is the heaviest reading on the sheet in either language, and it asks for nine or more numbers. A table lets my English learners show they found the numbers without first decoding the conditionals.
suggestion: Replace the Virginia line with a small table: rows Virginia, South Carolina and two states of the student's choice; columns 'with the clause / con la cláusula', 'counted in full / todas', 'not counted / ninguna'. Then ask one short question under it: 'Which states gained seats?'
evidence: English sheet question 3 answer prompt; 'Virginia: ___ seats with the three-fifths clause; ___ if counted in full; ___ if not counted at all.'

where: Question 3 step 1 ('Click Virginia and South Carolina') with the map's unlabeled states; Population layer pies
what: The sheet does not say to keep House seats in 1793 on for question 3. If it is off (or a class does only this question), there are no names at all and students must click around to find Virginia and South Carolina. The Massachusetts pie and the MA: 14 label sit in Maine, and the Maryland, Delaware and New Jersey pies overlap.
why: Students new to the country do not know the states by shape. Clicking through pop-ups to find two states is a lot of English reading before the real task starts.
suggestion: Start question 3 with 'Keep House seats in 1793 on and find the labels VA and SC.' Consider labeling the population pies with the state abbreviation too.
evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q1-bookmark.png (no names, pie in Maine, overlapping small pies); --q2-seats.png (MA: 14 in Maine)

where: Ratifying the Constitution pop-ups, first line (q4-delaware, q4-rhodeisland, q4-nc)
what: The line students are sent to read begins 'Ratified on 12/6/1787, 6:09 PM: 30 for, 0 against.' The date is in US number order, it carries a clock time that means nothing, and the teacher notes say it is a day early. The North Carolina pop-up adds 'voted 184 to 83 against ratifying', which is hard to untangle.
why: Spanish-speaking students read 12/6 as the 12th of June. The question only asks for the votes, but the date and time come first in the line and they will ask about them or copy them.
suggestion: Show the date in words with no time ('December 7, 1787') and put the votes first: '30 for, 0 against. Ratified December 7, 1787.' Reword the North Carolina note as '83 for, 184 against: it did not ratify.'
evidence: pop-up text: 'Ratified on 12/6/1787, 6:09 PM: 30 for, 0 against.'; 'A first convention, at Hillsborough in 1788, voted 184 to 83 against ratifying.'; teacher notes: 'Delaware shows 12/6/1787, not December 7'

where: Legend with each layer on (open, q2-seats, q4-ratify); pop-up wording (q2-delaware)
what: The legend headings are raw field names, 'Total1790' and 'HouseSeats', each layer has a grey 'Other' entry that is nowhere on the map, and the size scale reads '> 747,610 ... < 59,094'. The Delaware pop-up says 'That gave Delaware 1 House seats' and '1 seats'.
why: My students use the legend as their dictionary for the map. Headings that are not words, and an entry with nothing to match, add confusion; '1 seats' is the wrong model for learners of English.
suggestion: Rename the legend headings 'People in 1790', 'House seats' and 'Delegates who voted', remove 'Other', and fix the singular in the pop-up ('1 House seat').
evidence: legend text: 'Total1790', 'HouseSeats', 'Other'; pop-up text: 'That gave Delaware 1 House seats in 1793 ... counted in full: 1 seats.'

where: Both student sheets, Before you start and Reading the map; teacher notes, Key words
what: Ratify, convention, census, clause and seat are used on the sheet without a meaning, and the key words list in the teacher notes has no definitions and no Spanish. In the Spanish sheet 'escaños' is glossed against 'House seats' only once, and 'Compromiso' (Gran Compromiso, Compromiso de los Tres Quintos) in everyday Spanish means a commitment, not a deal where each side gives something up. Reading the map is one paragraph of about 118 words.
why: These are the words the whole lesson turns on. Without a meaning on the page, my students can do the clicks and still not know what a seat or ratifying is.
suggestion: Add a word box to both sheets: seat / escaño (un puesto en el Congreso), ratify / ratificar (aprobar oficialmente), census / censo, clause / cláusula, compromise / compromiso (acuerdo en que cada lado cede algo). Break Reading the map into one line per layer.
evidence: Teacher notes: 'Key words: ratify, convention, census, apportionment, Great Compromise, three-fifths clause, Federalist, Anti-Federalist'; Spanish sheet: 'Lo resolvieron con el Gran Compromiso y con el Compromiso de los Tres Quintos'

where: Spanish student sheet, question 4 step 1; lesson page note on the Spanish
what: Step 1 says 'En Map layers, desactiva Population in 1790 y House seats in 1793' with no Spanish for the tool, where every other step says 'En las capas del mapa (Map layers)'. The sheet uses short layer names (Population in 1790, Ratifying the Constitution) while the app lists 'Population in 1790: free and enslaved' and 'Ratifying the Constitution, 1787–1791'. The lesson page says the Spanish is a draft for review by a native speaker.
why: Small things, but my students match strings exactly, and I want to know the Spanish has been checked before I hand it out.
suggestion: Make step 1 match the others, use the full layer names as the app shows them, and complete the native-speaker review.
evidence: Spanish sheet: 'En Map layers, desactiva Population in 1790 y House seats in 1793.'; Map layers list in the packet; lesson page: 'Español: Spanish draft for review by a native speaker.'

where: Topographic basemap zoomed in on a town (q2-buildings); question 2 steps 1 and 2, question 3
what: Zoomed in on downtown Columbus 'until the basemap shows building names', the names that appear are an arena, colleges, a university, schools, a hospital, parks and a train station. I see no courthouse, city hall, library, place of worship, polling place or newspaper office, which are the six kinds of place the sheet lists. Polling places and newspaper offices would not be labeled on any basemap.
why: The step reads as if the map will show these places. Students who grew up here can fall back on what they know; my newcomers do not know where the courthouse or city hall is, so they have nothing to pin.
suggestion: Say plainly in step 2 that the basemap labels some buildings and students add others they know, and give the teacher a prompt to hand out three addresses or cross streets. List the label words students can actually expect (school, church, park, library, courthouse) and drop or explain polling place and newspaper office. A layer of public buildings would remove the problem.
evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q2-buildings.png (labels: Nationwide Arena, Columbus State Community College, Franklin University, Africentric School, Capitol Square; no courthouse, city hall or library); sheet: 'Zoom in on your town until the basemap shows building names.'

where: Spanish student sheet, question 2 step 2, question 3 step 1, question 4 answer
what: The kinds of building are given only in Spanish: 'un tribunal, el ayuntamiento, una biblioteca, un lugar de culto, un centro de votación o la redacción de un periódico', 'una oficina de correos'. On the basemap the labels are in English (Courthouse, City Hall, Library, Church, Post Office). Elsewhere the Spanish sheet gives the English map word beside the Spanish; here it does not. Library is also a false friend (librería is a bookshop).
why: Students must search the map for English words the sheet never shows them. This is the one place in the lesson where the Spanish-to-map match breaks.
suggestion: Add the English label after each: 'un tribunal (Courthouse), el ayuntamiento (City Hall), una biblioteca (Library), un lugar de culto (Church, Temple, Mosque, Synagogue), una oficina de correos (Post Office)'. 'La oficina de un periódico' is simpler than 'la redacción'.
evidence: Spanish sheet: 'Encuentra cuatro lugares públicos, no viviendas: un tribunal, el ayuntamiento, una biblioteca, un lugar de culto, un centro de votación o la redacción de un periódico.'

where: The map as it opens (open); question 1 step 1 'Zoom to your town'
what: The map opens on the whole United States with the country covered in thick blue district lines; most city names in the east are buried under them. The tool list has no search box, so 'zoom to your town' means finding it by eye from the national view.
why: Students who arrived recently often cannot place their town, or even their state, on a US map. This is the first step of the lesson and everything else depends on it.
suggestion: Suggest in Before class that the teacher shares a link already zoomed to the town, or put the town on the board with its state and nearest big city. In the sheet: 'Find your state first, then the nearest big city, then your town.' Thinner district lines at the national view would let the city names show.
evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--open.png (dense blue outlines over the eastern states); tool list in the packet has no search; sheet: 'Zoom to your town; the basemap has place names.'

where: Congressional districts layer zoomed out to a state (q1-state); question 1 step 4 and 'How many districts does your state have?'
what: At the state view the districts are outlines only, with no numbers, and the state border is the same blue as the district lines and runs on into the neighboring states' districts. Counting Ohio's districts by eye from this picture is hard; in a state with 28 or 52 it is not realistic.
why: It is a counting task that needs no English, which is good for my students, but the map does not let them count reliably, so the answers will all differ and I cannot tell who understood.
suggestion: Label each district with its number at state zoom, or change the question to 'click three districts in your state: what are their numbers?' and give the state's total in the teacher notes.
evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q1-state.png; answer notes: 'The district count is the number of blue-outlined areas in the state when zoomed out'

where: Both student sheets: Before you start, question 3; teacher notes question 3
what: Responsibilities are framed as a citizen's: 'Citizens also have responsibilities', 'a citizen's responsibility: voting, jury service, paying taxes' (responsabilidad ciudadana). The rights half never says that the Bill of Rights protects people who are not citizens too. Nothing in the teacher notes mentions students or families who are not citizens.
why: Many of my English learners and their parents are not citizens. Two of the three examples (voting, jury service) are things their families cannot do, while they do pay taxes and obey laws. As written, the lesson can leave them outside the 'we' in its title, and I would want to check the facts on who each right and duty applies to before teaching it.
suggestion: Use 'people who live here' or 'members of the community' where it is true, and add one line to the sheet: 'Most rights in the Bill of Rights protect everyone in the United States. Some responsibilities, such as voting and jury service, are for citizens; others, such as obeying laws and paying taxes, are for everyone.' Add a teacher note on handling this with care.
evidence: English sheet: 'Citizens also have responsibilities to their community and their country.'; 'Add a pin at each place where people carry out a citizen's responsibility: voting, jury service, paying taxes.'

where: Both student sheets, question 2 step 4 and question 3 step 3; Before you start
what: Step 4 says 'Next to each pin, write a right from the Bill of Rights', without saying whether that means a text label on the map (the teacher notes say 'add a text label') or on the sheet, or how to add text in Sketch. The rights themselves are named only in the short Before you start paragraph, in one language per sheet.
why: My students need the names of the rights in front of them, in both languages, to choose from; recalling 'due process' or 'freedom of assembly' cold in a second language is the hard part, not the mapping.
suggestion: Add a two-language word bank to both sheets (freedom of speech / libertad de expresión; freedom of religion / libertad de religión; freedom of the press / libertad de prensa; right to assemble / derecho de reunión; right to a fair trial / derecho a un juicio justo) and say 'write the right on your sheet, or add a text label in Sketch'.
evidence: English sheet: 'Next to each pin, write a right from the Bill of Rights that people use there.'; teacher step: 'Open Sketch, put a pin on it and add a text label.'

where: Spanish student sheet: Cómo leer el mapa, questions 2 and 3
what: Two wording problems. 'Los límites de los distritos del Congreso número 119 (2025–2027)' reads as if there were a district number 119, just before a question that asks '¿qué número tiene el distrito?'. And this sheet calls a pin 'marcador' ('Usa Sketch (dibujar) para colocar un marcador'), while the other sheets in the set use 'marcador' for a bookmark ('Abre el marcador ...') and 'alfiler' for a pin; this map also has a Bookmarks tool.
why: My students use the same Spanish sheets across the set, so a word that means bookmark on Monday and pin on Tuesday causes real confusion. The 119 could be written down as the district number.
suggestion: Write 'los distritos congresionales del 119.º Congreso (2025–2027)' or simply 'los distritos del Congreso actual'. Use 'alfiler' (or 'chincheta/pin') for pins everywhere and keep 'marcador' for Bookmarks.
evidence: Spanish sheet: 'Las líneas azules son los límites de los distritos del Congreso número 119 (2025–2027)'; 'Usa Sketch (dibujar) para colocar un marcador en cada uno.'; Vicksburg Spanish sheet: 'Abre el marcador The Battle of Vicksburg' and 'el alfiler amarillo'

where: National Register of Historic Places layer and pop-up (q4-nrhp, q4-nrhp-click); question 4
what: The diamonds are very small and nearly all the same dark green (building); the other legend colors are hard to tell apart at that size. The pop-up has the name and address at the top, which is clear, but then 'Property ID', 'Status: Listed' and 'National Register Information Tracking System Reference Number'. 'The two nearest your school' assumes students have found their school first, and the sheet does not say what to do if there are no diamonds nearby (the teacher notes do; I am inferring that some towns have none).
why: The useful lines are short, so this mostly works, but the extra lines are long official English that my students will try to read, and the school has to be found before the step can start.
suggestion: Trim the pop-up to name, address and Resource Type; make the diamonds larger. Add a step 'Find your school on the basemap first' and a line 'If there are none near your school, look in the town center.'
evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp.png; pop-up text: 'Property ID: 72001011 ... National Register Information Tracking System Reference Number: 72001011'

where: Spanish student sheet: Pregunta central, Tu respuesta; lesson page note on the Spanish
what: A few places where the Spanish is correct enough but not quite natural: the big question '¿Dónde, en nuestra comunidad, las personas ejercen sus derechos y cumplen sus responsabilidades?' keeps English word order; 'Elige los tres lugares que mejor muestran' should be 'que mejor muestren'; 'viviendas' is more formal than 'casas'. The lesson page marks the Spanish as a draft for native-speaker review.
why: Small, but this is the sheet I hand to students as a model of good written Spanish.
suggestion: '¿En qué lugares de nuestra comunidad ejercen las personas sus derechos y cumplen sus responsabilidades?'; 'los tres lugares que mejor muestren'; 'no en casas'. Finish the review and remove the draft note.
evidence: Spanish sheet lines quoted; lesson page: 'Español: Spanish draft for review by a native speaker.'

where: Spanish student sheet throughout (Antes de empezar, Cómo leer el mapa, all four questions); English sheet Before you start
what: The Spanish sheet uses 'electores' for electors and never says what one is. In everyday Spanish 'los electores' are the voters. So 'cómo votaron los electores de un estado' reads as 'how the state's voters voted', and the pop-up title 'Maryland: 10 electors' looks like ten voters. The English sheet does not explain elector either; the only explanation is in the teacher notes under Common misunderstandings.
why: This is the central word of the lesson and for my Spanish speakers it is a false friend that points to exactly the misunderstanding the teacher notes warn about ('Voters chose the president directly').
suggestion: Add one sentence to Before you start in both languages: 'Electors are not the voters. Each state chose a small group of people, called electors, to vote for president.' / 'Los electores no son los votantes: cada estado elegía a un pequeño grupo de personas, los electores (Colegio Electoral), para votar por el presidente.'
evidence: Spanish sheet: 'Cada gráfico muestra cómo votaron los electores de un estado'; pop-up title: 'Maryland: 10 electors'; teacher notes: '“Voters chose the president directly.” Electors did'

where: The sixteen states bookmark with either election layer (q1-courts-off, q2-1800); questions 1 and 3 ('which part of the country', 'check New England')
what: The map has no names at all: sixteen pies on blank outlines. The questions ask which part of the country voted for each man and whether any New England state changed (fíjate en Nueva Inglaterra), but nothing on the map or sheet says which states are New England, or names North, South or West. The Massachusetts pie sits up in Maine.
why: Students who have been in the country a year or two do not know the states by shape or which ones make up New England. They can see orange at the top and blue at the bottom, but they cannot name it without clicking all sixteen pies and already knowing the regions.
suggestion: Label each pie with its state abbreviation, as the House seats layer in the We the People map does. In the sheet, name the New England states once ('New England: New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, the five orange pies in the north-east') and offer answer words: north / norte, south / sur, west / oeste.
evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--q1-courts-off.png and --q2-1800.png (no labels); sheet: 'Find the states whose pies changed their shares, and check New England.'

where: Election pop-ups (q1-pie, q1-maryland, q2-pennsylvania, q4-newyork); questions 1, 2 and 4
what: The first line lists four or five names with numbers ('John Adams 7, Thomas Jefferson 4, Thomas Pinckney 4, Aaron Burr 3, others 2') under a title that says '10 electors', so the numbers add up to 20. The 1800 pop-ups put Jefferson and Burr first with equal numbers and add a paragraph about the 73 to 73 tie, the House vote and the 12th Amendment. The second paragraph repeats the two numbers students need ('In the pie: ...') but it comes after a sentence about votes adding up to twice the electors, and reads '1 votes'.
why: My students need two numbers per state. They have to find them among four names in a paragraph, and the '73 votes each' for Jefferson and Burr collides with the sheet's 'Jefferson 73, Adams 65' in question 4.
suggestion: Put the two pie numbers first and on their own lines ('Adams: 7' / 'Jefferson: 4'), then the other candidates in smaller text. In the sheet add: 'Read only the numbers for Adams and Jefferson.' Fix '1 votes'.
evidence: pop-up text: 'Electors' votes in 1796: John Adams 7, Thomas Jefferson 4, Thomas Pinckney 4, Aaron Burr 3, others 2.'; 'In the pie: John Adams (Federalist), 1 votes'; 'Jefferson and Aaron Burr tied with 73 votes each'

where: The map as it opens (open, q1-bookmark); Landmark Supreme Court cases layer; question 1 step 2
what: The map opens with two pink squares and a long label, 'Marbury v. Madison (1803)', sitting on top of Maryland's pie, and the legend starts with that layer. The sheet's first job is to turn off a layer this lesson never uses. Its name, 'Landmark Supreme Court cases, 1803 and 1819', is the one layer name the Spanish sheet does not translate in the step.
why: It is an extra step and the longest English name on the sheet, before the lesson has started. A student who misses it gets a court case pop-up when they click Maryland, which is one of the four states question 1 is about.
suggestion: Have the court cases layer off when the map opens (the stretch task can turn it on). If it stays on, gloss it in the Spanish step: '(casos históricos de la Corte Suprema)'.
evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--open.png (pink squares and label over Maryland); Spanish sheet: 'desactiva Landmark Supreme Court cases, 1803 and 1819: sus cuadrados rosados tapan el gráfico de Maryland.'

where: Maryland, Delaware and New Jersey pies at the bookmark view (q1-courts-off, q2-1800); legend
what: The pies for Maryland, Delaware and New Jersey overlap each other, so a click there can open a neighbor (the sheet's '1 of 2' tip covers this). The legend has a grey 'Other' entry that matches nothing on the map.
why: Maryland is the closest state in 1800 and the answer to 'which state was the closest', so it is the pie students most need to click cleanly.
suggestion: Nudge the Delaware and New Jersey pies apart or shrink the smallest pies slightly, and remove 'Other' from the legend.
evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--q2-1800.png (overlapping pies near Maryland); legend text: 'Other'

where: Both student sheets, question 3 answer prompt; Spanish sheet, Reflexión; lesson page note on the Spanish
what: Question 3's answer prompt packs three questions into one paragraph with one fill-in line. In the Spanish Looking back, 'Si hubieras podido cambiar el resultado ..., ¿cuál elegirías?' mixes tenses; it should be '¿cuál habrías elegido?'. The lesson page marks the Spanish as a draft for native-speaker review.
why: Three questions in a row is where my English learners answer the first and stop. The tense slip is small, but I notice it and so will my stronger Spanish readers.
suggestion: Split question 3's prompt into a, b and c, each with its own line. Change the Spanish to '¿cuál habrías elegido, y por qué?' and complete the review.
evidence: English sheet question 3 answer prompt; Spanish sheet: 'Si hubieras podido cambiar el resultado en un solo estado en 1800, ¿cuál elegirías, y por qué ese?'; lesson page: 'Español: Spanish draft for review by a native speaker.'

where: Spanish student sheet, Cómo leer el mapa; affects question 2 (Why New Orleans?), steps 2 and 3
what: The English Reading the map ends with 'Watersheds shows larger regions when you zoom out and smaller ones when you zoom in.' The Spanish paragraph stops at 'muestran el paisaje actual' and leaves that sentence out.
why: Question 2 has no bookmark step, so a student who has zoomed in gets small watersheds with other names instead of Ohio Region and Missouri Region. My English-sheet students are warned; my Spanish-sheet students are not, and they are the ones least able to work out what went wrong.
suggestion: Add the sentence to the Spanish sheet: 'Watersheds muestra regiones más grandes cuando alejas el mapa y más pequeñas cuando lo acercas.' Better still, start question 2 in both sheets with 'Open The Louisiana Purchase bookmark'.
evidence: English: 'Watersheds shows larger regions when you zoom out and smaller ones when you zoom in.' Spanish paragraph ends: 'Las capas United States Watersheds y Biomes están desactivadas al abrir el mapa y muestran el paisaje actual.'

where: q2-watersheds picture, United States Watersheds layer; question 2 step 2 (English and Spanish)
what: The step says to click inside the two large brown outlines along the Ohio River and the Missouri River. With the layer on I see about twenty brown outlines across the whole country, no river names and no place names, and the rivers themselves are faint on the basemap.
why: A student who arrived in the United States recently does not know where the Ohio or the Missouri is, in either language. Nothing on the map tells them which two outlines are meant, so they click at random or wait for me.
suggestion: Use what is on the map to point: 'Click inside the brown outline that holds the eastern part of the trail (the Ohio River), then the outline that holds the long north-west part of the trail (the Missouri River).' Or add the two river names as labels.
evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q2-watersheds.png; sheet: 'Click inside the two large brown outlines along the Ohio River and the Missouri River.' / 'Haz clic dentro de los dos grandes contornos marrones junto al río Ohio y al río Misuri.'

where: Spanish student sheet, question 4 (A través de las Montañas Rocosas), step 2 and the Responde line
what: 'Busca dónde sale la línea de la ruta de la compra de Luisiana, en amarillo' and '¿Dónde sale la línea de la ruta de la compra de Luisiana?' read at first as 'the line of the route of the Louisiana Purchase', as if the purchase had a route.
why: It is grammatical but a student has to read it twice to see that the trail line is leaving the yellow area. For a struggling reader that is the whole question lost.
suggestion: Reword: 'Busca el lugar donde la línea de la ruta sale de la zona amarilla (la compra de Luisiana).' and '¿En qué lugar sale la ruta de la zona amarilla de la compra de Luisiana?'
evidence: Spanish sheet: 'Busca dónde sale la línea de la ruta de la compra de Luisiana, en amarillo.'; '¿Dónde sale la línea de la ruta de la compra de Luisiana?'

where: Spanish student sheet, all questions: the tool names
what: Map layers and Measure are given in English with a gloss ('Map layers (capas del mapa)', 'Measure (medir)'), but Legend and Bookmarks never are: the sheet only says 'usa la leyenda' and 'Abre el marcador'. The order of English and Spanish also flips ('Map layers (capas del mapa)' in question 2, 'las capas del mapa (Map layers)' in question 4, and no English at all in question 3 step 3).
why: The buttons in the app say Legend and Bookmarks. My students match words on the sheet to words on the screen; where the English word is missing they cannot find the button.
suggestion: Give every tool once in the same pattern, English first: 'Bookmarks (marcadores)', 'Legend (leyenda)', 'Map layers (capas del mapa)', 'Measure (medir)', ideally in one line at the top of Cómo leer el mapa.
evidence: Spanish sheet: 'Abre el marcador The Louisiana Purchase (La compra de Luisiana) y usa la leyenda.'; 'En Map layers (capas del mapa), activa...'; 'En las capas del mapa, desactiva United States Watersheds...'; 'En las capas del mapa (Map layers), desactiva Biomes'

where: q4-pittsburgh picture, Lewis and Clark campsites layer; question 4 steps 3 and 4 (Measure)
what: The sheet says to find the trail's eastern end at Pittsburgh. Zoomed out, the line of dots ends in western Pennsylvania, but five or six more campsite dots sit further east, near the Chesapeake, with no line joining them. Nothing is labeled Pittsburgh.
why: A student told to find 'the eastern end' ('el extremo este') will reasonably pick the dots furthest east. Their measurement then comes out longer and may fall outside the accepted 2,100 to 2,300 miles, and they will not know why.
suggestion: Say on the sheet: 'the eastern end of the continuous line of dots (not the few separate dots further east)'. Or label Pittsburgh on the map, or remove the detached eastern campsites.
evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q4-pittsburgh.png (isolated orange dots at the right edge, east of where the line stops); sheet: 'find the trail's eastern end at Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, where the Ohio River begins'

where: q3-biomes and q3-biome-click pictures, Biomes layer legend and pop-up; question 3 answer
what: The answer to '¿Qué bioma cubre las Grandes Llanuras?' is an English phrase, 'Temperate Grasslands, Savannas & Shrublands', with no gloss on the Spanish sheet. In the legend its swatch looks the same tan as Mangroves, the legend has 16 entries and this one is at the bottom of what shows, and the pop-up goes on with 'Realm: Nearctic' and a paragraph headed 'Nature Could Recover'.
why: My English learners can copy the phrase but will not know it means grassland, so the second half of the question (why follow rivers across open country) has nothing to hang on. The extra pop-up text is hard and has nothing to do with the lesson.
suggestion: On the Spanish sheet add a gloss: 'el nombre está en inglés; grasslands = pastizales o praderas'. On the English sheet add '(grassland)'. If the layer allows it, trim the pop-up for this map to the biome and ecoregion lines.
evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q3-biomes.png (Mangroves and Temperate Grasslands swatches both tan); pop-up text: 'Temperate Grasslands, Savannas & Shrublands / Realm: Nearctic / Ecoregion: Northern Shortgrass prairie / Nature Could Recover ...'

where: Teacher notes: Key words, Support and stretch; student sheets
what: The key words (watershed, river basin, biome, Continental Divide, expedition) are a bare list for the teacher. None is explained on the student sheet in either language, 'Continental Divide' is never used on the sheet, and the Spanish gloss for watersheds, 'cuencas hidrográficas', is itself a hard term for grade 8. The Support line has nothing for English learners.
why: I check whether key words are supported. Here I would have to write my own word bank before the lesson.
suggestion: Add one plain sentence each to Before you start, as the land cessions and 1828 lessons do: 'A watershed is all the land whose water drains into one river.' / 'Una cuenca es toda la tierra cuya agua va a dar a un mismo río.' Offer a short English–Spanish word list in the teacher notes.
evidence: Teacher notes: 'Key words: Louisiana Purchase, Corps of Discovery, expedition, watershed, river basin, biome, Continental Divide, Tribal Nation'; Spanish sheet: 'United States Watersheds (cuencas hidrográficas)'

where: Spanish student sheet, small wording points; lesson page note under the sheet
what: Small things in otherwise good Spanish: the sheet writes 'río Misuri' and 'Misisipi' while the map pop-up says 'Missouri Region'; '4900 millas' has no comma where the English sheet and the pop-up use them ('4,900', '530,000,000'); 'su reclamación sobre' is correct but 'su reclamo' is what most of my students would say. The lesson page also still says 'Spanish draft for review by a native speaker'.
why: None of these stops a student, but each is a small mismatch between the sheet and the screen, and I cannot tell from the page whether the review has happened.
suggestion: Give the English spelling once in brackets ('río Misuri (Missouri)'), write 4,900 to match the map, and update or remove the draft note once a native speaker has reviewed it.
evidence: Spanish sheet: 'La ruta mide unas 4900 millas.'; 'Río Misuri arriba'; pop-up: 'Missouri Region'; lesson page: 'Español: Spanish draft for review by a native speaker.'

where: open and q1-bookmark pictures, Territorial acquisitions and trail layers; Reading the map / Cómo leer el mapa
what: The sheet calls the 1783 land green ('verde'); on the map it is a dark gray-teal. The 'purple line' ('línea morada') is almost completely hidden under the orange-red campsite dots, and the sheet never says what color the campsite symbols are.
why: Color words are the easiest words for my students, so they lean on them. When the color on screen is not the color on the sheet they stop trusting the sheet. The legend label is long English ('Territory of the Original Thirteen States (Ceded by Great Britain) 1783').
suggestion: Say 'gray-green' / 'verde grisáceo', and describe the trail as it looks: 'a line of orange-red dots (campsites) with a thin purple line under it' / 'una fila de puntos rojo-anaranjados (campamentos) sobre una línea morada fina'.
evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--open.png; louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q1-bookmark.png; sheet: 'green is the land Britain gave up', 'A purple line follows the Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail'

where: q4-mexico and q4-colombia pictures, Latin American independence and US recognition pop-ups; question 4 steps 3 and 4
what: The recognition date shows as '12/11/1822, 6:09 PM' for Mexico and '6/18/1822, 6:09 PM' for Colombia. The answer notes give December 12 and June 19, so the pop-up is a day early, with a clock time that means nothing. The sheet says the pop-up 'gives the exact date'.
why: My Spanish-speaking students read 12/11/1822 as 12 November: at home the day comes first. So they are comparing a wrong day, in a format they misread, against '2 de diciembre de 1823' written out. The which-side-of-the-message answer still comes out right, but their dates will not match the answer key and the 6:09 PM invites questions I cannot answer. The teacher notes admit the problem; the sheet does not.
suggestion: Fix it on the map: show the date as text ('December 12, 1822') from a text field rather than a date-time field. Until then add to both sheets: 'The date is written month/day/year; ignore the time.' / 'La fecha está escrita mes/día/año; no hagas caso de la hora.'
evidence: war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q4-mexico.png: 'Recognized by the United States: 12/11/1822, 6:09 PM.'; war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q4-colombia.png: '6/18/1822, 6:09 PM'; answer notes: 'Mexico (December 12, 1822)', 'Mexico shows 12/11/1822, not December 12'

where: q4-latin picture, Latin American independence and US recognition layer labels; question 4 step 3
what: At the Latin America in 1825 bookmark the blue circle on the coast of Brazil has no label of its own; the nearest label is 'Paraguay 1811'. The 'Federation of Central America 1821' label floats over Cuba, far from its circle, and partly covers Haiti's diamond. Under all this the old basemap prints its own names (Peru beside Paraguay, Aruba, Guayana, Saint-Domingue).
why: My students know this map of the world better than the map of the United States, so they will notice. A student listing 'the blue circles' from the labels writes Paraguay as recognized by 1824 and never finds Brazil. They can fix it by clicking, but only if they suspect the label.
suggestion: Make Brazil's label show at this bookmark's scale and anchor each label on its own symbol (or use callout lines). Tell students on the sheet to take the nation's name from the pop-up title, not from the nearest label.
evidence: war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q4-latin.png (blue circle right of the 'Paraguay 1811' label; no 'Brazil' layer label; 'Federation of Central America 1821' over the Caribbean); answer notes: 'Six blue circles ... Brazil (May 26, 1824)'

where: Legend and battle pop-ups (open, q1-bookmark, q2-neworleans pictures); Spanish sheet Cómo leer el mapa and questions 1 and 2
what: The Spanish sheet explains the diamonds only in Spanish: 'azul si ganaron los estadounidenses, rojo si ganaron los británicos y gris si ningún bando ganó ... más bajas'. On screen the words are American Victory, British Victory, Inconclusive, Total Casualties and, in the pop-up, 'American Side Victory'. The English labels are not given beside the Spanish, though layer and bookmark names are.
why: My students have to match the sheet to the screen. 'Casualties' is a trap for Spanish speakers because it looks like 'casualidades' (coincidences), and 'bajas' in this sense is not a word many 13-year-olds know either. 'Inconclusive' has no clue at all.
suggestion: Add the legend words in brackets: 'azul: American Victory (ganaron los estadounidenses); rojo: British Victory; gris: Inconclusive (ningún bando ganó); Total Casualties = bajas: muertos, heridos, capturados y desaparecidos'. Define casualties on the English sheet too.
evidence: Legend text: 'American Victory / British Victory / Inconclusive / Total Casualties'; pop-up: 'American Side Victory', 'Total Casualties: 2,096'; Spanish sheet: 'los rombos más grandes indican más bajas'

where: Battle pop-ups (q1-detroit, q1-chesapeake, q2-lundyslane pictures); question 1 step 2 and question 2 step 2
what: The sheet says 'read their pop-ups' and 'Work out where from the map and the pop-up's account'. Under the three useful lines, each pop-up is a long English essay: Lundy's Lane runs to eight paragraphs of military writing ('countermanded', 'flank', 'point-blank melee of musketry'), River Raisin to five.
why: An English learner told to read the pop-up will try to read all of it and lose ten minutes on one battle. To say where a battle was, they must find a place name buried in that text, because the pop-up has no state line and the map has no state names.
suggestion: Change the step to 'Read only the top three lines: the dates, who won, and Total Casualties' / 'Lee solo las tres primeras líneas'. For 'where', let students describe the place from the map (by the Great Lakes, on the Gulf coast) and say so on the sheet, or add a State line to the pop-up.
evidence: Pop-up text for Lundy's Lane (about 700 words) and River Raisin; sheet: 'Click some diamonds in each group and read their pop-ups.'; 'Work out where from the map and the pop-up's account.' / 'Deduce dónde a partir del mapa y del relato de la ventana emergente.'

where: q3-boundary and q3-florida-east pictures; question 3 step 3 (English and Spanish)
what: Step 3 says 'Click the green land and read its pop-up. Drag the map east to see all of Florida.' At The 1819 boundary bookmark the view is the West: the only green in sight is a sliver in the Rockies and a strip at the far right edge. Florida only appears after dragging. And 'drag the map east' / 'Arrastra el mapa hacia el este' is unclear: to see land that lies to the east you pull the map to the left.
why: The steps are in the wrong order for what the bookmark shows, and the teacher's From the front has them the other way round (drag first, then click). My students follow steps literally; they will click the sliver in Colorado or drag the wrong way.
suggestion: Reorder and reword: 'Move the map until you can see all of Florida, in the south-east corner (drag the map to the left). Then click the green land in Florida and read its pop-up.' / 'Mueve el mapa hasta ver toda Florida, en la esquina sureste (arrastra el mapa hacia la izquierda). Luego haz clic en la tierra verde de Florida.' Or add a Florida bookmark.
evidence: war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q3-boundary.png; war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q3-florida-east.png; From the front: 'Drag the map east until all of Florida shows, click the green land'

where: Reading the map / Cómo leer el mapa (both sheets)
what: Reading the map is one unbroken paragraph of about 150 words that explains six layers, eight colors and shapes, a warning about the legend's 'British' label and which layers are off. The Spanish is accurate but just as dense.
why: This is the heaviest block of reading on the sheet and it comes before any question. My English learners need it most and are least likely to get through it.
suggestion: Set it out as a short key, one line per symbol, in both languages: pink shading = United States in 1800; blue diamond = American Victory; and so on, with the three off layers listed under the question that uses them.
evidence: English sheet Reading the map: 'The map has no place names: click a feature to see its name. Pink shading shows ... the pop-up gives the exact date.' (one paragraph)

where: open, q1-bookmark and q4-latin pictures, basemap; Reading the map first sentence; answer notes for question 1
what: The sheet says 'The map has no place names' / 'El mapa no tiene nombres de lugares', and the answer notes repeat it. The basemap does print names: United States, Louisiana, New Spain of Mexico, Cuba, Bahamas, Saint-Domingue, Brazil. What it lacks is states, cities, lakes and rivers.
why: The first sentence of the instructions is contradicted by the first thing on screen. It also matters for question 2, which sends students to 'the Niagara River, between Lake Erie and Lake Ontario': none of those three is named on the map.
suggestion: Say 'The map names countries as they were in 1800, but not states, cities, lakes or rivers'. For question 2 point with the map: 'zoom in on the biggest diamond, on the strip of land between two of the Great Lakes'.
evidence: war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--open.png (labels 'Louisiana', 'United States', 'New Spain of Mexico', 'Cuba'); sheet: 'The map has no place names: click a feature to see its name.'

where: q3-florida picture, Land Spain gave up in 1819 pop-up; question 3 first answer
what: The Florida pop-up is one long sentence pair: 'negotiated the acquisition of the Florida territory from Spain via the Adams-Onis Treaty ... they did agree to assume $5 million in damage caused by American citizens when they rebelled against Spain'. The answer notes say the last part is not what the treaty says.
why: 'Acquisition', 'via' and 'assume $5 million in damage' are hard for an English learner, and the one fact they work to decode is, by the lesson's own account, wrong.
suggestion: Rewrite the note in plain, correct words: 'In the Adams-Onís Treaty of 1819 Spain gave Florida to the United States. The United States paid Spain nothing, but agreed to pay up to $5 million that American citizens said Spain owed them.'
evidence: Pop-up text: 'While the Americans didn't pay Spain for the land, they did agree to assume $5 million in damage caused by American citizens when they rebelled against Spain'; answer notes: 'the treaty's own terms are claims by American citizens against Spain'

where: Spanish student sheet, question 3 Responde line, Tu respuesta, and Cómo leer el mapa
what: A few Spanish sentences are correct but awkward: '¿Dónde sigue la nueva frontera ríos y dónde sigue líneas rectas? ¿Por qué podría una frontera pasar de unos a otras?' (the student has to work out that 'unos' is rivers and 'otras' is lines); 'usando una batalla y una capa posterior' (later in time, or lower in the list?). The treaty line is 'rayas rosadas' in Cómo leer el mapa and 'línea discontinua rosada' in question 3.
why: These are exactly the sentences a weaker reader stalls on, and the two names for one line make them look for two things.
suggestion: '¿En qué partes la nueva frontera sigue un río y en qué partes sigue una línea recta? ¿Por qué crees que cambia de una forma a la otra?'; 'usando una batalla y una de las capas de 1819 o de América Latina'; use 'línea rosada de rayas' in both places.
evidence: Spanish sheet: '¿Por qué podría una frontera pasar de unos a otras?'; 'usando una batalla y una capa posterior'; 'rayas rosadas, en siete tramos' vs 'línea discontinua rosada'

where: Legend in the open and q4-latin pictures; pop-up title for the Río de la Plata nation
what: The legend's smallest casualties class reads '< 0', the recognition layer has a gray 'Other' entry that no sheet explains, and Argentina appears as 'Buenos Ayres'.
why: My students will ask what fewer than zero casualties means and whether 'Ayres' is a spelling mistake. Small, but each is a question that takes me away from another student.
suggestion: Relabel the smallest class (for example 'fewer than 100'), remove the 'Other' entry, and show 'Buenos Ayres (today Argentina; spelled this way in 1823)' in the label or note it on the sheet.
evidence: Legend text: 'Total Casualties > 2,628 / 2,000 / 1,300 / 700 / < 0'; 'Recognized by the United States by 1824 / Recognized later (1826 to 1862) / Other'; war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q4-latin.png label 'Buenos Ayres 1816'

where: Teacher notes: Key words, Support and stretch
what: The key words list has impressment and blockade, which never appear on the student sheet, and leaves out the words the sheet and map do lean on: casualties, victor, inconclusive, recognized, cession. Nothing in Support is aimed at English learners.
why: I look for key-word support. The list does not match what my students will meet on screen.
suggestion: Make the key words the ones on the sheet and legend, each with a one-line meaning and a Spanish equivalent (casualties = bajas; recognized = reconoció; treaty = tratado).
evidence: Teacher notes: 'Key words: impressment, blockade, Treaty of Ghent, cession, boundary, recognition, Monroe Doctrine, independence'

where: Lesson page Student activity; teacher notes Word file, Before class
what: There is no Spanish student sheet: the page offers only 'Download Word (English)' and the prompt box says 'Languages: student sheets in English'. But the Word teacher notes say 'The lesson includes the map, a two-page Word student sheet in English and Spanish'.
why: I use the Spanish sheet beside the English one for about a quarter of my class. This is the lesson with the hardest reading of the four (two quotations from the 1830s, source criticism), so it is the one where they need it most, and the notes promise something that is not there.
suggestion: Add the Spanish sheet in the same style as the Louisiana and War of 1812 ones (English layer and bookmark names with a gloss). Until then, correct the teacher notes to say English only.
evidence: Lesson page: '[Button: Download Word (English)]' only; prompt text: 'Languages: student sheets in English.'; teacher notes Word: 'a two-page Word student sheet in English and Spanish'

where: q1-us picture, The United States bookmark; question 1 steps 1 and 2 and answer (a); also question 5
what: Question 1 opens The United States bookmark and asks students to name three states with light blue. At that zoom the map shows city names (Chicago, St. Louis, Atlanta, Dallas) and 'UNITED STATES', but no state names. State names only appear at The Southeast and The Old Northwest bookmarks.
why: Students who went to elementary school in another country do not know the states by shape. They cannot answer (a) from this view, and the step that would help (The Southeast) comes after and is aimed at part (c).
suggestion: Add to step 2: 'Zoom in one or two steps until the state names show', or answer (a) from The Southeast and The Old Northwest bookmarks and keep The United States view for (b), the big empty part.
evidence: land-cessions-1784-1894--q1-us.png (no state labels); land-cessions-1784-1894--q1-southeast.png (MISSISSIPPI, ALABAMA, GEORGIA labeled); teacher notes: 'State names, cities and rivers are labeled above the colored areas'

where: Student sheet: Before you start, question 4 answer (b), question 6 answer (c)
what: The sheet carries two period quotations: Jackson's 'opening the whole territory between Tennessee on the north and Louisiana on the south to the settlement of the whites' (printed twice) and the petition's 'without any authority from the council or people of the Nation'. Question 4(b) is a 60-word question with the quotation inside it. 'Removal', 'settlement', 'authority', 'council' and 'petition' are not explained, though treaty and cession are.
why: With no Spanish sheet, these are the sentences my English learners cannot get past alone, and they carry the 'why' of the whole lesson.
suggestion: Follow each quotation with a plain-English line: 'In other words: Jackson wanted this land opened for white settlers.' 'In other words: the signers said the treaty-makers had no right to speak for the Cherokee Nation.' Add removal and petition to the definitions in Before you start, and split 4(b) into two short questions.
evidence: Sheet question 4: '(b) In December 1830 Jackson told Congress that removal meant "opening the whole territory between Tennessee on the north and Louisiana on the south to the settlement of the whites." Using his words and the Indian Removal Act (Before you start), why might these cessions have come in the 1830s, and why here?'

where: q4-choctaw picture and pop-up; question 4 step 3 and the fill-in line
what: The fill-in asks for 'the nation, the date, and the words on the first link' with one small blank for the date. The Choctaw pop-up captured shows 'Date or dates: November 16, 1805; September 27, 1830' and 'Today's states: Alabama'. (The capture opened a small Choctaw piece near the Alabama line, not the large area north-east of Jackson, so I cannot see what the large one says; the answer notes give September 27, 1830 only.)
why: Reading the map tells students to 'read every date', but the blank wants one, and the sheet does not say which. There are also several small orange Choctaw pieces around the big one, so a student's click may land on a different record from the one in the answer notes.
suggestion: Say in step 3: 'write the date in the 1830s'. In step 2 say 'the large orange area' as From the front does. Worth checking on the live map what the large area's pop-up shows for dates and states.

where: Pop-ups (q1-newyork, q1-maryland, q6-pennsylvania pictures and text); sheet Reading the map and question 4(a)
what: The wording leans on idioms: the sheet says 'pies' for the circles and 'on the same terms as white men'; the pop-ups say 'Shut out by a law of 1801', 'had already eased the rules', 'were excused', 'kept Black men from voting'. where: Student sheet, Before you start

where: Railroads in operation by 1863 with battlefields on, at the Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania bookmark and zoomed to Manassas and Petersburg; sheet question 5

where: Basemap at the bookmark (q1-bookmark); sheet question 2 'which side of the river'; teacher notes, common misunderstandings

where: Population and House seats pop-ups, third paragraph and source line (q1-virginia, q3-southcarolina); sheet question 3
what: The pop-up states 'If enslaved people had been counted in full: 22 seats. If they had not been counted at all: 13 seats.' and the source line under it says 'Seats: National Archives - Ratio: U.S. Census Bureau'. The 19 is a historical fact. The 22 and 13 are somebody's arithmetic: they assume Congress would have kept the same 33,000 ratio and the same rounding under a different count. Nothing in the pop-up says that.
why: If a parent asks 'who says Virginia would have had 13 seats?', the honest answer is 'the map's authors worked it out', and the pop-up reads as if the National Archives said so. For this topic I need calculated numbers labelled as calculated.
suggestion: Reword the paragraph: 'Worked out at the same ratio of one seat per 33,000: counted in full, 22 seats; not counted at all, 13 seats.' Add 'What-if seats: calculated by the map's authors' to the source line and one sentence in the notes showing the sum (630,559 divided by 33,000 is 19 and a fraction, and fractions were dropped).

where: Big question 'Who was counted in the new Constitution'; student sheet 'Before you start'; answer notes and model answer
what: The big question asks who was counted, and the lesson answers for free and enslaved people. It never says that the same clause left out 'Indians not taxed', so most Native people were not counted at all, and it does not say that the blue 'free people' slice includes free Black people and women and children who could not vote either. The lesson also never states which side at the Convention wanted the full count and which wanted none.
why: Native nations are one of the things my district looks for, and here a single sentence would do it. Without the 'who wanted what' line, students tend to read 'counted in full' as the generous option, when the pop-up's own numbers show it would have given slaveholding states even more seats.
suggestion: Add to the teacher notes, and in one short sentence to 'Before you start': the count for seats was free persons plus three-fifths of enslaved people, 'excluding Indians not taxed'. Add a misunderstanding line: 'Counting in full would have been fairer to enslaved people' with the correction that delegates from slaveholding states asked for the full count and many Northern delegates wanted none, and that being counted gave no vote.
evidence: Sheet: 'Big question: Who was counted in the new Constitution, and how close did it come to being rejected?' Legend: 'Free people / Enslaved people / Other'. No mention of Native people anywhere in the lesson page, sheet, notes or pop-ups.

where: Legends (open, q2-seats, q4-ratify); pop-up date style
what: The legend headings are raw field names: 'Total1790', 'HouseSeats', 'Total'. Each pie legend also has a grey 'Other' with nothing grey on the map. The sample pie in the population legend is drawn half blue, half orange-red. Dates inside pop-ups are written day first ('3-7 December 1787') while the first line uses 12/6/1787.
why: Students ask what 'Other' people are, on a map about who was free and who was enslaved, and I have no answer. The rest is polish, but it is the polish a review committee notices.
suggestion: Rename the headings ('People in 1790', 'House seats', 'Delegates voting'), remove the 'Other' entry, and use one American date style throughout ('December 3-7, 1787').
evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--open.png legend: 'Free people / Enslaved people / Other / Total1790'; --q2-seats.png: 'HouseSeats'; --q4-ratify.png: 'Voted to ratify / Voted against / Other / Total'.

where: Congressional districts (119th Congress) pop-up (q1-district); sheet 'Reading the map' and question 1; answer notes question 1

where: Student sheet question 3 step 2; standards table TX 8.19(C); answer notes question 3

where: Student sheet 'Before you start' and question 2 step 2; answer notes question 2
what: Two wordings I would be asked about. The sheet lists a 'place of worship' among 'public places' and has each student pin one; it does not say it can be any place of worship, not their own. why: A screenshot of a student's map with their own church, mosque or temple pinned is a record of the family's religion that I collected. And I have students who are not citizens; the sheet as worded tells them this lesson is about somebody else.
suggestion: Reword step 2 to 'any place of worship in your town (it does not have to be one you attend)' and call the list 'places open to the community' rather than 'public places'. where: Student sheet question 4 and Before you start; Answering the compelling question; model answer
what: The student sheet never says what the Monroe Doctrine said; that is only in my notes. where: Student sheet Before you start and question 4(b); answer notes for question 4
what: The standard says 'analyze the reasons' for removal. The sheet gives students one reason, a single clause from Jackson's December 1830 message about 'the settlement of the whites', and the accepted answer is 'Jackson's own reason'. Jackson's message gave other stated reasons too, and the sheet does not give the name of the document for either quotation (the message or the 1836 petition); those are only in my notes. Before you start says the Act let the President 'move' nations and never says the moves were forced or that people died.
why: A parent on one side will say the lesson picked the one line that makes Jackson look worst; a parent on the other will say 'move' hides what happened. With one quotation and no document names on the sheet I cannot show either of them that students weighed the evidence.
suggestion: Add a second stated reason from the same message so students weigh reasons, name both documents on the sheet (title, date, National Archives), and add one factual sentence that removal was carried out by force for many, with the source already in the notes. I would check both quotations word for word against the DocsTeach transcriptions, and the 3,352 figure.

where: Standards table: TX 8.5(G) and TX 8.10(A)

where: Big question, questions 3 to 6, Answering the compelling question and the model answer
what: The lesson sets up 'a victory for the common man' and then every piece of evidence it gives students cuts against it; the model answer ends '1828 was a victory for more white men, but not for everyone the common man might include'. The only evidence for the other side is in question 5 (voters choosing electors for the first time in three states). There is nothing on how the rules had changed since 1800 or how many more men voted in 1828 than 1824. Enslaved people are an expected answer in question 6(b) but are never mentioned on the sheet.
why: The facts are sourced and I can defend each one. What I cannot easily defend is a lesson where the conclusion looks decided in advance: that is the complaint I would get, and the standard itself says 'expanded suffrage'.
suggestion: Give students sourced evidence for the expansion as well: for example how many states had dropped property rules for white men since 1800, and the rise in votes cast from 1824 to 1828, then let them weigh it. Reword the model answer so it shows both sides before concluding. Add one factual sentence to Before you start that enslaved people could not vote anywhere.
